steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A data type defines the kind of data a variable can hold. Choosing the correct data type ensures data is stored efficiently and prevents errors.

steps.title: Integer
steps.body: stores whole numbers only - no decimal points. Use integer for counts, ages, positions, and any value that cannot logically be fractional.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Storing 3.14 as an integer would lose the decimal part, storing only 3. If a value needs decimal precision, use Real/Float instead.

steps.title: Real (or Float)
steps.body: stores numbers with a decimal point. Use real for measurements, prices, averages, and scientific calculations where precision matters.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Name the five main data types and give an example value for each. | What is the difference between the integer 7 and the string "7"? | What is the result of INT("25") + INT("10")?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Integer: 42, Real/Float: 3.14, Boolean: TRUE, Character: 'A', String: "Hello". | The integer 7 can be used in mathematical operations (7 + 3 = 10). The string "7" is text and would concatenate ("7" + "3" = "73"). They are stored and processed differently. | INT("25") = 25, INT("10") = 10, so 25 + 10 = 35.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Know all five data types and be able to give appropriate examples Use single quotes for characters ('A') and double quotes for strings ("Hello") Remember INT() truncates - it does NOT round INPUT usually returns a string - you must cast it for arithmetic When asked why data types matter, mention memory, validation, and correct operations Be careful with + operator: it adds numbers but concatenates strings
